# Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document analyzes Directive 2003/87/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 October 2003 establishing a scheme for greenhouse gas emission allowance trading within the Community and amending Council Directive 96/61/EC, Official Journal L 275, 25/10/2003. *Source: Directive 2003/87/EC, European Parliament and Council, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003L0087.* The captured text is the base 2003 directive as consolidated on EUR-Lex; it does not include the text of later amending acts extending the scheme to aviation or maritime transport, which are outside this document's grounded scope. This document is scoped to the provisions the captured text grounds: the permit and allowance-trading obligations on installation operators, the free-allocation method, the annual surrender and verification cycle, and the excess-emissions penalty regime.

# What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The Directive, adopted by the European Parliament and the Council, establishes what the text calls the "Community scheme" for trading greenhouse gas emission allowances among operators of stationary installations carrying out the activities listed in the Directive's Annex I. "This Directive establishes a scheme for greenhouse gas emission allowance trading within the Community (hereinafter referred to as the "Community scheme") in order to promote reductions of greenhouse gas emissions in a cost-effective and economically efficient manner." *Source: Directive 2003/87/EC, European Parliament and Council, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003L0087.* The scheme, as captured, covers stationary industrial and energy-generation installations, not freight transport operations directly. For workspaces whose clients operate energy-intensive facilities in scope (power generation, combustion plants, and other Annex I activities), the Community scheme sets a cost the client bears on its own emissions, which can feed into the pricing of goods the workspace moves. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any workspace-controlled site (a warehouse, distribution centre, or other facility with a combustion source) meets an Annex I activity and capacity threshold and would itself become an "installation" whose operator holds duties under the Directive; the captured text renders the Annex I activity and threshold table as a stripped table with no cell values, so the specific thresholds cannot be confirmed from this pool.

# Issues Requiring Immediate Action

**COST ALERT.** Assess whether any client that operates an Annex I installation is exposed to the excess emissions penalty regime, since an operator that does not surrender sufficient allowances "shall be held liable for the payment of an excess emissions penalty." *Source: Directive 2003/87/EC, European Parliament and Council, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003L0087.* *Operational implication:* a client's excess-emissions exposure or its allowance-purchase cost under the Community scheme can flow into the pricing of goods and shipment volumes the workspace handles on that client's behalf, though the specific pass-through mechanism to any individual client requires client-specific data. *Analytical inference:* effect on cost of goods produced by ETS-covered installations requires client-specific and installation-specific data.

**MONITORING.** Confirm, before treating any workspace facility as outside scope, whether it meets an Annex I activity and capacity threshold; the captured text does not carry the threshold values, only the general aggregation rule for installations on the same site. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any workspace-controlled site is an "installation" within the meaning of the Directive.

# How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The Directive's duty holders are "operators" of installations carrying out Annex I activities: the party that "operates or controls an installation or, where this is provided for in national legislation, to whom decisive economic power over the technical functioning of the installation has been delegated." *Source: Directive 2003/87/EC, European Parliament and Council, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003L0087.* A freight forwarder that neither owns nor controls an Annex I installation does not fall within this duty-holder class on the captured text. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any workspace activity or facility places it within the "operator" definition rather than remaining an unaffected third-party carrier moving goods to or from a client's covered installation.

# Substantive Requirements

**Permit obligation.** From the scheme's operative date, an installation may not undertake an Annex I activity without an emissions permit: "Member States shall ensure that, from 1 January 2005, no installation undertakes any activity listed in Annex I resulting in emissions specified in relation to that activity unless its operator holds a permit issued by a competent authority in accordance with Articles 5 and 6, or the installation is temporarily excluded from the Community scheme pursuant to Article 27." *Source: Directive 2003/87/EC, European Parliament and Council, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003L0087.*

**Free-allocation trajectory.** The proportion of allowances Member States must issue free of charge steps down over two defined periods: "For the three-year period beginning 1 January 2005 Member States shall allocate at least 95 % of the allowances free of charge." and, for the following period, "For the five-year period beginning 1 January 2008, Member States shall allocate at least 90 % of the allowances free of charge." *Source: Directive 2003/87/EC, European Parliament and Council, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003L0087.* *Analytical inference:* the step from 95% to 90% free allocation between the two periods is the qualification a headline "free allocation" figure alone would omit; the text does not state a further step beyond the second period in the captured pool.

**Annual surrender and excess-emissions penalty.** An installation operator surrenders allowances annually and faces a fixed per-tonne penalty on any shortfall: "Member States shall ensure that, by 30 April each year at the latest, the operator of each installation surrenders a number of allowances equal to the total emissions from that installation during the preceding calendar year as verified in accordance with Article 15, and that these are subsequently cancelled." "The excess emissions penalty shall be EUR 100 for each tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent emitted by that installation for which the operator has not surrendered allowances." A lower transitional rate applied during the first period: "During the three-year period beginning 1 January 2005, Member States shall apply a lower excess emissions penalty of EUR 40 for each tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent emitted by that installation for which the operator has not surrendered allowances." *Source: Directive 2003/87/EC, European Parliament and Council, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003L0087.* Payment of the penalty does not discharge the underlying allowance obligation for the following year.

**Verification gate on transfers.** An operator whose emissions report is not verified as satisfactory cannot transfer allowances: "Member States shall ensure that an operator whose report has not been verified as satisfactory in accordance with the criteria set out in Annex V by 31 March each year for emissions during the preceding year cannot make further transfers of allowances until a report from that operator has been verified as satisfactory." *Source: Directive 2003/87/EC, European Parliament and Council, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003L0087.*

# Registration and Reporting Obligations

An installation's permit application is submitted to the competent authority describing the installation and its activities, the raw and auxiliary materials likely to lead to emissions, the emission sources, and the planned monitoring and reporting measures. Each operator reports its installation's emissions to the competent authority after the end of each calendar year, and Member States themselves report to the Commission on the Directive's application, with "the first report shall be sent to the Commission by 30 June 2005." *Source: Directive 2003/87/EC, European Parliament and Council, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003L0087.* *Operational implication:* these are installation-operator duties; the workspace's own registration burden, if any, depends on whether it separately meets the "operator" definition assessed above.

# Operational System Requirements

For workspaces with clients operating Annex I installations: (1) confirm the client's permit and allowance-account status before treating shipment volumes tied to that installation's output as unaffected by allowance costs, and (2) track the client's annual surrender cycle, since a verification failure or a shortfall against emissions carries the fixed per-tonne penalty above. *Operational implication:* neither duty creates a direct system build for the forwarder itself, since the duty holders are the installation operators, not the carrier moving their goods.

# Confirmed Regulatory Timeline

- 13 October 2003: Directive 2003/87/EC adopted by the European Parliament and the Council at Luxembourg; the Directive enters into force on the day of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. *Source: Directive 2003/87/EC, European Parliament and Council, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003L0087.*
- 1 January 2005: the permit requirement takes effect; no installation may undertake an Annex I activity without an operator-held emissions permit, and the first three-year allocation period (at least 95% free allocation) begins. *Source: Directive 2003/87/EC, European Parliament and Council, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003L0087.*
- 1 January 2008: the second, five-year allocation period begins, with the free-allocation floor stepping down to at least 90%. *Source: Directive 2003/87/EC, European Parliament and Council, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003L0087.*

# Sources

- Directive 2003/87/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 October 2003, Official Journal L 275, 25/10/2003 (Tier 1, primary binding text). https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003L0087

# Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document analyzes the Road Traffic (Vehicle Emissions) (Fixed Penalty) Regulations 1997 (S.I. 1997 No. 3058), made under the Environment Act 1995. *Source: The Road Traffic (Vehicle Emissions) (Fixed Penalty) Regulations 1997, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1997/3058.* This document is scoped to the provisions the captured original-as-made text grounds: the fixed penalty notice scheme for vehicle smoke-emission and stationary-idling offences, the amounts and escalation of the fixed penalty, and the hearing and enforcement procedure. The captured text is the original 1997 version; it does not include any subsequent amendment.

# What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The Regulations create a fixed penalty notice scheme, administered by named local authorities, for two vehicle-emissions offences: contravention of regulation 61 of the Road Vehicles (Construction and Use) Regulations 1986 (smoke and other substances emitted from vehicles) and contravention of regulation 98 of those Regulations (stopping the engine of a stationary vehicle to avoid noise and exhaust emissions). "These Regulations make provision for specified local authorities to issue fixed penalty notices to users of vehicles within their area who contravene, or fail to comply with, regulation 61 of the Road Vehicles (Construction and Use) Regulations 1986 and to drivers of vehicles within their area who contravene, or fail to comply with, regulation 98 of those Regulations." *Source: The Road Traffic (Vehicle Emissions) (Fixed Penalty) Regulations 1997, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1997/3058.* For workspaces operating their own road fleet, or contracting road haulage, into or within the named participating authority areas, drivers and vehicle users are the persons directly exposed to these fixed penalty notices. *Operational implication:* the scheme covers only the seven named participating authority areas below, not UK-wide road use; exposure is geographically bounded to operations within those areas.

# Issues Requiring Immediate Action

**COST ALERT.** Assess whether the workspace's own vehicles, or subcontracted road haulage moving on its behalf, operate within any of the seven participating authority areas, since a smoke-emission or stationary-idling contravention there carries a fixed penalty escalating on non-payment. *Source: The Road Traffic (Vehicle Emissions) (Fixed Penalty) Regulations 1997, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1997/3058.* *Analytical inference:* effect on cost of road-fleet operations requires operator-specific route and vehicle-condition data.

**MONITORING.** Confirm the current escalated fixed penalty amounts and participating-authority list against the latest available (revised) version on legislation.gov.uk, since this document is grounded only in the original-as-made text. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any later amendment has changed the fixed penalty amounts, the offence definitions, or the list of participating authorities since 1997.

# How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The duty to avoid the underlying offences under regulation 61 and regulation 98 of the 1986 Regulations falls on "the person using" the vehicle for the smoke-emission offence and on the driver for the stationary-idling offence; the fixed penalty notice itself is issued to that person, not to a third party arranging the carriage. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace, where it subcontracts road haulage rather than operating its own fleet, has any exposure beyond its own directly operated vehicles and drivers under this instrument.

# Substantive Requirements

**Fixed penalty amounts.** The fixed penalty is set by offence type, "subject to regulation 9": "(i) of £60 in the case of a fixed penalty offence relating to regulation 61 of the 1986 Regulations, or (ii) of £20 in the case of a fixed penalty offence relating to regulation 98 of the 1986 Regulations;" *Source: The Road Traffic (Vehicle Emissions) (Fixed Penalty) Regulations 1997, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1997/3058.*

**Escalation on non-payment.** Where the fixed penalty is not paid within the payment period and no hearing has been requested, the amount is increased: "(a) to £90, in the case of an offence relating to regulation 61 of the 1986 Regulations, and (b) to £40, in the case of an offence relating to regulation 98 of the 1986 Regulations." *Source: The Road Traffic (Vehicle Emissions) (Fixed Penalty) Regulations 1997, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1997/3058.* *Analytical inference:* the escalation is the qualification a headline £60/£20 figure alone would omit; the real exposure on late payment is £90/£40, half again to double the original amount.

**Payment window and hearing right.** The person notified may pay within the period for paying or instead request a hearing: "the period for paying" in relation to any fixed penalty notice, means the period of 28 days beginning with the day on which the notice was issued." Requesting a hearing suspends the fixed penalty: "Where a hearing has been requested in accordance with paragraphs (1) and (2), the fixed penalty shall not be payable." *Source: The Road Traffic (Vehicle Emissions) (Fixed Penalty) Regulations 1997, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1997/3058.*

**Notice content.** A fixed penalty notice states the name and address of the person to whom it is issued, the vehicle's registered number, the date of the offence, the monetary amount, payment details, and the consequences of non-payment. *Source: The Road Traffic (Vehicle Emissions) (Fixed Penalty) Regulations 1997, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1997/3058.*

# Registration and Reporting Obligations

This instrument creates no separate registration or periodic-reporting scheme; its own administrative record is the fixed penalty notice, whose required content is addressed in Substantive Requirements above. *Operational implication:* no ongoing filing burden attaches to the workspace beyond responding to an individual notice if one is issued.

# Operational System Requirements

For workspaces operating vehicles within the seven participating authority areas: (1) brief drivers on regulation 61 (smoke) and regulation 98 (stationary-idling) compliance, since an authorised person may require a driver's name, address, and date of birth in connection with enforcement, and (2) establish an internal process for handling a fixed penalty notice within its 28-day payment window, including the decision whether to request a hearing. *Operational implication:* the 28-day window is short relative to typical internal review cycles, so a fast-track escalation path to the workspace's compliance function reduces the risk of missing the window and triggering the increased penalty.

# Confirmed Regulatory Timeline

- 19th December 1997: The Road Traffic (Vehicle Emissions) (Fixed Penalty) Regulations 1997 made by the Secretary of State; coming into force on the seventh day after the day on which they are made. *Source: The Road Traffic (Vehicle Emissions) (Fixed Penalty) Regulations 1997, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1997/3058.*

# Sources

- The Road Traffic (Vehicle Emissions) (Fixed Penalty) Regulations 1997, S.I. 1997 No. 3058, UK Government, legislation.gov.uk (Tier 1, primary binding text, original as made). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1997/3058

# Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document analyzes Council Regulation (EC) No 1420/1999 of 29 April 1999 establishing common rules and procedures to apply to shipments to certain non-OECD countries of certain types of waste, Official Journal L 166, 01/07/1999. *Source: Council Regulation (EC) No 1420/1999, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31999R1420.* This document is scoped to the provisions the captured text grounds: the country-by-country export prohibition and control-procedure regime for waste destined for recovery in non-OECD countries, and the review mechanism. The full country lists in Annex A and Annex B (over 100 countries and territories each) are addressed illustratively, not exhaustively, in this document; the workspace should confirm any specific destination against the current Annex A/B listing directly.

# What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The Regulation, adopted by the Council of the European Union, sets export controls, additional to Council Regulation (EEC) No 259/93 on waste shipments, for exports of recovery-destined waste (Annex II to Regulation (EEC) No 259/93) from the Community to non-OECD countries that either objected to receiving such waste or never responded to the Commission's inquiry. Countries objecting are listed in this Regulation's own Annex A, where export "shall be prohibited"; countries that did not respond are listed in Annex B, where the Article 15 (Regulation (EEC) No 259/93) prior-notification control procedure applies instead of an outright ban. *Source: Council Regulation (EC) No 1420/1999, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31999R1420.* For workspaces arranging export shipments of recovery-destined waste, scrap metal, or similar recyclable materials to any of the listed non-OECD destinations, this Regulation determines whether that shipment is banned outright or merely subject to a prior-notification procedure. *Operational implication:* the Regulation's own recitals note certain non-EU obligations layer on top of this list; recital 10 records that Article 39 of the Fourth ACP-EC Convention already bars export of Basel Convention Annex I and II waste to ACP countries, and this Regulation excludes those items from its own scope because they are already covered by that separate prohibition.

# Issues Requiring Immediate Action

**ACTION REQUIRED.** Screen the destination country of any recovery-destined waste export against this Regulation's Annex A before accepting the booking: an Annex A-listed country and waste type combination is an outright export ban, not a documentation matter. *Source: Council Regulation (EC) No 1420/1999, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31999R1420.* *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace, acting as freight forwarder rather than the waste exporter of record, carries any liability exposure under the Member State's national implementing penalty regime for facilitating a prohibited export; the captured text specifies no penalty provision of its own.

**MONITORING.** For an Annex B-listed destination, confirm the Article 15 (Regulation (EEC) No 259/93) prior-notification control procedure has been completed before shipment; the specific notification and consent documentation mechanics are defined in that separate Regulation, not in this captured text. *Operational implication:* Annex A and Annex B are subject to the Commission's own periodic review, so a destination's status can change between shipments.

# How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The Regulation's own operative articles address exports "from the Community"; the party arranging or effecting the export (the waste exporter of record) is the party the underlying control and prohibition regime targets. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace, in a freight-forwarding or customs-broker capacity rather than as the waste exporter itself, falls within the scope of any Member State penalty provision implementing this Regulation and Regulation (EEC) No 259/93; the captured text names no penalty mechanism of its own for this document to ground a role determination against.

# Substantive Requirements

**Annex A prohibition.** "The export of waste listed in Annex II to Regulation (EEC) No 259/93 and mentioned in Annex A to this Regulation to countries listed in said Annex A shall be prohibited." *Source: Council Regulation (EC) No 1420/1999, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31999R1420.*

**Annex B control procedure.** "The control procedure laid down in Article 15 of Regulation (EEC) No 259/93 shall apply to exports to the countries listed in Annex B to this Regulation with respect to those categories of waste destined for recovery only and listed in Annex II to Regulation (EEC) No 259/93." *Source: Council Regulation (EC) No 1420/1999, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31999R1420.*

**Country-requested change of procedure.** A destination country may ask the Commission to change which control procedure applies to it; the Commission then notifies Member States "within 21 days of receipt of the request" and submits a proposed determination to the relevant committee "within three months of receipt of the request." *Source: Council Regulation (EC) No 1420/1999, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31999R1420.* *Analytical inference:* the qualification a headline "control procedure applies per Annex" statement would omit is that the specific procedure for an Annex B country can be reassigned mid-cycle at that country's own request, on this 21-day/three-month administrative timeline.

**ACP country exclusion.** Waste items already covered by the Fourth ACP-EC Convention's own export prohibition (Basel Convention Annex I and II waste to ACP countries) are excluded from this Regulation's own scope, since that separate international obligation already bars the shipment. *Source: Council Regulation (EC) No 1420/1999, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31999R1420.*

**Illustrative country entries.** Annex A country entries are typically drawn narrowly by waste sub-category rather than blanket bans: for example, the Annex A entry for "ALBANIA" reads "All types except:" a list of specific ferrous and non-ferrous metal scrap and other sub-categories carved out from the prohibition, and the Annex B entry for "ANGOLA" similarly reads "All types except:" a shorter list of carved-out sub-categories. *Source: Council Regulation (EC) No 1420/1999, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31999R1420.* *Analytical inference:* a workspace cannot rely on a country's presence on Annex A or Annex B alone; the specific waste sub-category carve-outs for that country determine whether a given shipment is banned, controlled, or unrestricted.

# Registration and Reporting Obligations

The Annex B control procedure incorporates Article 15 of Regulation (EEC) No 259/93 by reference; the specific notification form and consent documentation for that procedure are set out in that separate Regulation, not in the captured text of this instrument. *Specific notification-form details not available from primary sources as of the export date.*

# Operational System Requirements

For workspaces arranging recovery-destined waste exports: (1) build a destination-country screening step against the current Annex A and Annex B listings before booking, and (2) track the Commission's periodic review of those Annexes, since a country's status is not fixed. *Operational implication:* the specific waste sub-category carve-outs mean this cannot be a single country-level yes/no gate; the screening step needs waste-category granularity to match Annex A and Annex B's own structure.

# Exemptions and Edge Cases

Most Annex A and Annex B country entries carry sub-category carve-outs rather than a blanket ban or blanket control procedure: the source text's own qualifying language is "All types except:" followed by the specific waste sections excluded from the country's general prohibition or control status. Some countries (for example ANDORRA, GHANA, or CAPE VERDE in Annex A) carry no carve-out at all, so "All types" of the covered Annex II waste is banned for that destination. *Source: Council Regulation (EC) No 1420/1999, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31999R1420.*

# Confirmed Regulatory Timeline

- 29 April 1999: Council Regulation (EC) No 1420/1999 adopted at Luxembourg; the Regulation enters into force on the 90th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Communities, and is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States. *Source: Council Regulation (EC) No 1420/1999, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:31999R1420.*

# Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document analyzes the Single Use Carrier Bags Charge (Wales) Regulations 2010 (Welsh Statutory Instrument 2010 No. 2880 (W.238)), made under the Climate Change Act 2008, as captured in its latest available (revised) consolidated form. *Source: The Single Use Carrier Bags Charge (Wales) Regulations 2010, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2010/2880.* This document is scoped to the provisions the captured consolidated text grounds: the minimum per-bag charge, the seller definition and its delivery-based territorial reach, the record-keeping and publication duties, the exemptions in Schedule 1, and the civil-sanctions penalty regime in Schedules 2 to 4.

# What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The Regulations, made by the Welsh Ministers, set a minimum charge that a "seller" must apply to every new single use carrier bag supplied with goods sold from, or delivered to, Wales. Critically, "seller" is defined by the destination of the goods, not only the seller's own location: "sells goods from a place in Wales; (b) sells goods which are delivered to persons in Wales." *Source: The Single Use Carrier Bags Charge (Wales) Regulations 2010, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2010/2880.* For workspaces operating or supporting e-commerce fulfilment, warehousing, or last-mile delivery into Wales on behalf of a client, this delivery-based scope means the charge duty can attach even when the point of sale is outside Wales. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace, where it fulfils or delivers orders on a client's behalf rather than selling in its own right, is itself the "seller" under regulation 4, or whether that duty remains with the client on whose behalf the workspace is acting; regulation 4(2) states that where a person sells goods as an officer or employee of another, the other person is the seller, a structure that may or may not extend to a third-party fulfilment relationship on the facts.

# Issues Requiring Immediate Action

**COST ALERT.** Confirm whether any workspace-supported delivery or fulfilment operation into Wales involves supplying new single use carrier bags with the goods, since a qualifying bag must carry the minimum charge and an unpaid or under-charged bag is a breach carrying a civil sanction. *Source: The Single Use Carrier Bags Charge (Wales) Regulations 2010, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2010/2880.* *Operational implication:* the specific per-shipment cost of applying the charge correctly depends on client-specific packaging practice and is not something this document can quantify without that data.

**MONITORING.** Confirm whether any client the workspace fulfils for meets the reporting-year threshold (ten or more full-time-equivalent staff on the first day of the reporting year) that brings Part 3 record-keeping and publication duties into play, and separately the 1,000-bag annual threshold that brings the publication duty specifically into play. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace's own fulfilment role could itself trigger these thresholds if it is found to be the "seller" for the relevant goods.

# How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The duty to charge, keep records, and publish records under Parts 2 and 3 falls on the "seller" as defined in regulation 4; a workspace acting purely as carrier or freight forwarder, without selling the goods in its own right, sits outside that definition on its face. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a workspace providing fulfilment, pick-pack, or last-mile delivery services that itself selects and applies the carrier bag at the point of dispatch to a Welsh address could be treated as exercising the "seller" function under regulation 4, particularly where the workspace, rather than the retail client, controls bag selection and charging at the point of dispatch.

# Substantive Requirements

**Minimum charge.** "The amount that a seller must charge is such amount as ensures that the consideration paid by a customer for each single use carrier bag is not less than 5 pence." *Source: The Single Use Carrier Bags Charge (Wales) Regulations 2010, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2010/2880.*

**Record-keeping and retention.** A seller keeps a record of specified information (bag counts, consideration received, net proceeds and their use) for every reporting year once the ten-or-more-staff threshold is met, and "Records must be retained by a seller for a period of three years beginning on 31 May in the reporting year following that to which a record relates." *Source: The Single Use Carrier Bags Charge (Wales) Regulations 2010, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2010/2880.*

**Publication threshold and deadline.** Publication of the record is required only once a seller is a VAT-taxable person and separately meets a volume threshold, "that the seller supplies 1000 or more single use carrier bags which attract the charge," and where required, "a seller must publish the record on or before 31 May in the reporting year following that to which the record relates." *Source: The Single Use Carrier Bags Charge (Wales) Regulations 2010, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2010/2880.* *Analytical inference:* the qualification a headline "sellers must publish records" statement would omit is that publication is threshold-gated on both VAT-taxable status and the 1,000-bag volume test, so a smaller-volume seller has no publication duty even if it keeps records.

**Civil sanctions.** For failure to comply with the core charging requirement, Schedule 2's penalty table states the row "Failure to comply with the requirement to charge in accordance with regulation 6 (regulation 11(1) and (2)) £200 £100" (fixed monetary penalty, discounted specified sum). A more serious category of breach carries a substantially higher variable monetary penalty exposure, per the row "Without reasonable cause, giving false or misleading information to an administrator (regulation 11(3)) £20,000". A seller may discharge its liability early at a discount, or face an increase if it delays: "A seller may discharge its liability to a fixed monetary penalty by paying 50% of the amount of the penalty within 28 days beginning with the day on which the final notice imposing it was received." "If a fixed monetary penalty is not paid within the period allowed in accordance with paragraph 8 the amount of the penalty is increased by 50%." *Source: The Single Use Carrier Bags Charge (Wales) Regulations 2010, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2010/2880.*

# Threshold Questions

The threshold question this Regulation turns on for a logistics or fulfilment workspace is whether it is a "seller" under regulation 4, since every substantive duty (charge, record-keeping, publication) attaches only to that defined role. The regulation's own text defines "seller" by reference to who sells the goods, including by delivery destination, and separately provides that an officer or employee selling on behalf of another person is not themselves the seller. *Legal Confirmation Required:* how this defined-role test applies to a third-party fulfilment or last-mile delivery arrangement where the workspace, not the retail client, physically selects and charges for the bag at the point of dispatch; this document states what the text defines and does not resolve that fact-specific determination.

# Registration and Reporting Obligations

There is no separate registration scheme; the operative obligations are the record-keeping duty (triggered by the ten-or-more-staff threshold) and the publication duty (triggered additionally by the 1,000-bag volume threshold and VAT-taxable status), both addressed in Substantive Requirements above. *Operational implication:* a seller below both thresholds carries no record-keeping or publication duty under this instrument, though the underlying charging duty still applies regardless of size.

# Operational System Requirements

For workspaces supporting delivery or fulfilment of goods into Wales: (1) confirm with each client whether the workspace or the client is treated as the "seller" applying the charge, and (2) where the workspace's own operations meet the ten-or-more-staff or 1,000-bag thresholds in its own right, build the record-keeping and, where triggered, publication process described above. *Operational implication:* the courier-bag exemption addressed in Exemptions and Edge Cases below may remove the charge question entirely for pure delivery-packaging use, which is the scenario most relevant to a freight or logistics workspace's own bag use.

# Exemptions and Edge Cases

Schedule 1 exempts a defined list of bag types from the charge. Two exemptions are directly relevant to freight and logistics operations: bags used to package goods for onward carriage, and delivery-service bags. The Schedule's own text states one relevant exemption as "(i) mail order dispatch and courier bags;" meaning a bag used purely for mail-order or courier dispatch, rather than a retail carrier bag handed to a shopper, falls outside the charge requirement entirely. *Source: The Single Use Carrier Bags Charge (Wales) Regulations 2010, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2010/2880.* A separate, later-added exemption for bags used in grocery delivery or collection services is time-limited rather than permanent: that exemption applies "only until midnight on 31 December 2020," after which grocery-delivery bags returned to being subject to the ordinary charge and record-keeping regime described above. *Analytical inference:* the sunset on the grocery-delivery exemption is the qualification a headline "delivery bags are exempt" reading would omit; by the current (revised) text, that specific carve-out no longer applies.

# Confirmed Regulatory Timeline

- 30 November 2010: The Single Use Carrier Bags Charge (Wales) Regulations 2010 made by the Welsh Ministers. *Source: The Single Use Carrier Bags Charge (Wales) Regulations 2010, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2010/2880.*
- 1 October 2011: The Regulations come into force in relation to Wales, and the substituted charging and record-keeping provisions take effect. *Source: The Single Use Carrier Bags Charge (Wales) Regulations 2010, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2010/2880.*
- 31 December 2020: The time-limited grocery-delivery and collection bag exemption ends. *Source: The Single Use Carrier Bags Charge (Wales) Regulations 2010, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2010/2880.*

# Sources

- The Single Use Carrier Bags Charge (Wales) Regulations 2010, S.I. 2010 No. 2880 (W.238), UK Government, legislation.gov.uk (Tier 1, primary binding text, latest available revised consolidated version). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2010/2880

# Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document analyzes the U.S. Department of Energy final rule "Application for Authorization To Transmit Electric Energy to a Foreign Country," Federal Register Volume 91, Number 118 (Monday, June 22, 2026), FR Doc No. 2026-12475, amending 10 CFR part 205. *Source: DOE final rule, Application for Authorization To Transmit Electric Energy to a Foreign Country, Federal Register. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/22/2026-12475/application-for-authorization-to-transmit-electric-energy-to-a-foreign-country.* This document is scoped to the provisions the captured text grounds: the simplified application requirement for cross-border electricity export authorization under Federal Power Act section 202(e), and the fee elimination adopted alongside it. This instrument governs export authorization for electric energy itself, not the carriage of goods or equipment; its relevance to a freight-forwarding workspace is narrow and indirect, addressed under Compliance Chain below.

# What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The rule, issued by DOE's Office of Electricity, finalizes a simplification of the application process a "person" must follow to obtain authorization to transmit electric energy from the United States to a foreign country: "To obtain authorization to transmit any electric energy from the United States to a foreign country, an electric utility or any other person seeking to transmit any electricity from the U.S. to a foreign country must submit an application or be a party to an application submitted by another entity." *Source: DOE final rule, Application for Authorization To Transmit Electric Energy to a Foreign Country, Federal Register. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/22/2026-12475/application-for-authorization-to-transmit-electric-energy-to-a-foreign-country.* *Operational implication:* this rule addresses the authorization to transmit electricity itself (a utility or power-marketer function), not the transport of goods, cargo, or grid equipment; a freight-forwarding workspace has no direct duty under this rule unless it is itself the applicant seeking export authorization, which is not the ordinary freight-forwarding role. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any workspace activity supporting a client's cross-border electricity export project (for example, logistics for grid-interconnection equipment tied to an authorized export arrangement) creates any obligation of its own under this rule; the captured text names only the electricity exporter as the applicant.

# Issues Requiring Immediate Action

**MONITORING.** Note the rule's effective date and reduced application burden for any client the workspace serves in the cross-border electricity trading or grid-interconnection sector, since that client's own authorization costs and timeline have changed. *Source: DOE final rule, Application for Authorization To Transmit Electric Energy to a Foreign Country, Federal Register. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/22/2026-12475/application-for-authorization-to-transmit-electric-energy-to-a-foreign-country.* *Analytical inference:* effect on the workspace's own logistics volumes tied to any such client's export activity requires client-specific data this document does not have.

# How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The applicant under this rule is "an electric utility or any other person seeking to transmit any electricity from the U.S. to a foreign country"; a freight forwarder moving goods or equipment is not itself transmitting electricity and does not fall within this applicant class on the captured text. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace, in a role supporting a client's cross-border transmission or interconnection project, has any reporting or documentation obligation under 10 CFR part 205 distinct from the electricity exporter's own application duty; the captured text names no such distinct role.

# Substantive Requirements

**Simplified application content.** The final rule replaces a detailed, multi-section application requirement with a single provision: the application "shall include information the applicant deems relevant to DOE's determination under section 202(e) in the Federal Power Act," and the prior detailed requirements at 10 CFR 205.301 through 205.309 are removed and reserved. *Source: DOE final rule, Application for Authorization To Transmit Electric Energy to a Foreign Country, Federal Register. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/22/2026-12475/application-for-authorization-to-transmit-electric-energy-to-a-foreign-country.*

**Statutory approval standard, unchanged.** DOE's approval standard under the underlying statute is not altered by this rule: "shall issue such order [authorizing the export of electricity to a foreign country] upon application unless, after opportunity for hearing, it finds that the proposed transmission would impair the sufficiency of electric supply within the United States or would impede or tend to impede the coordination in the public interest of facilities subject to the jurisdiction of [DOE]." *Source: DOE final rule, Application for Authorization To Transmit Electric Energy to a Foreign Country, Federal Register. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/22/2026-12475/application-for-authorization-to-transmit-electric-energy-to-a-foreign-country.*

**Fee elimination.** "It also reduces the financial burden placed on applicants by eliminating the $500 application filing fee, which is estimated to reduce the annual application burden by $10,000." *Source: DOE final rule, Application for Authorization To Transmit Electric Energy to a Foreign Country, Federal Register. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/22/2026-12475/application-for-authorization-to-transmit-electric-energy-to-a-foreign-country.* *Analytical inference:* the qualification a headline "$10,000 burden reduction" figure would omit is that this is an aggregate estimate across all applicants (DOE estimates about 20 applications per year), not a per-application saving of that size.

# Registration and Reporting Obligations

The rule imposes no new information-collection requirement of its own: DOE states the final rule "imposes no new information collection requirements subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act and OMB clearance is not required." *Source: DOE final rule, Application for Authorization To Transmit Electric Energy to a Foreign Country, Federal Register. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/22/2026-12475/application-for-authorization-to-transmit-electric-energy-to-a-foreign-country.* *Operational implication:* the registration and reporting burden here runs to the electricity exporter applicant, not to any logistics or freight-forwarding party supporting that exporter's project.

# Operational System Requirements

For a workspace that serves clients in cross-border electricity trading, transmission, or grid-interconnection equipment logistics: (1) note that the client's application process is now simplified and DOE's opportunity-for-hearing practice going forward is publication of notice on DOE's website or in the Federal Register rather than the FERC Rule 211/214 protest-and-intervention process DOE previously used voluntarily, and (2) confirm whether any timing change to a client's authorization affects a scheduled shipment of interconnection or transmission equipment. *Operational implication:* this document has no basis to quantify any specific shipment-timing effect without client-specific project data.

# Confirmed Regulatory Timeline

- May 16, 2025: DOE published the notice of proposed rulemaking (NOPR) on this application-process simplification, opening a public comment period. *Source: DOE final rule, Application for Authorization To Transmit Electric Energy to a Foreign Country, Federal Register. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/22/2026-12475/application-for-authorization-to-transmit-electric-energy-to-a-foreign-country.*

# Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document analyzes Decision of the EEA Joint Committee No 15/2003 of 31 January 2003 amending Annex XX (Environment) to the EEA Agreement, Official Journal L 094, 10/04/2003. *Source: Decision of the EEA Joint Committee No 15/2003, EEA Joint Committee, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:22003D0015.* This is a short incorporation instrument: it extends two Commission Decisions issued under Directive 2000/53/EC on end-of-life vehicles (ELVs) into the EEA Agreement, so that they also apply as between the EU and the EEA EFTA states (Iceland, Norway, Liechtenstein). The captured text does not itself restate the substantive content of the two incorporated Decisions; it only identifies them and brings them into EEA law.

# What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The EEA Joint Committee decided to insert two Commission Decisions into Annex XX of the EEA Agreement: "Commission Decision 2001/753/EC of 17 October 2001 concerning a questionnaire for Member States reports on the implementation of Directive 2000/53/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council on end-of-life vehicles(2) is to be incorporated into the Agreement." and a second Decision "on minimum requirements for the certificate of destruction issued in accordance with Article 5(3) of Directive 2000/53/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council on end-of-life vehicles(3) is to be incorporated into the Agreement." *Source: Decision of the EEA Joint Committee No 15/2003, EEA Joint Committee, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:22003D0015.* *Operational implication:* this instrument's own text is administrative incorporation, not a substantive obligation; the operative content a workspace handling end-of-life vehicles would need (the certificate-of-destruction minimum requirements themselves) sits in Commission Decision 2002/151/EC, which this pool does not carry beyond its title and citation. For workspaces engaged in the automotive vertical, particularly cross-border movement or deregistration of vehicles at end of life, the certificate of destruction referenced here is the document that ends a vehicle's registration in an EEA member state.

# Issues Requiring Immediate Action

**MONITORING.** Where the workspace handles end-of-life vehicle movements into or within the EEA, confirm the current certificate-of-destruction requirements directly from Commission Decision 2002/151/EC, since this incorporation instrument names but does not restate that Decision's substantive minimum requirements. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any workspace vehicle-handling activity brings it within the reporting or documentation duties Directive 2000/53/EC and its implementing Decisions impose on Member State authorities and authorised treatment facilities, as distinct from a carrier moving a vehicle that is not yet at end of life.

# How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The duty holders under the incorporated Decisions are Member States (for the reporting questionnaire) and the authorities or facilities issuing certificates of destruction (for the minimum-requirements Decision); a freight forwarder moving vehicles is not itself a duty holder under either incorporated Decision on the captured text. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace's own role in an end-of-life vehicle's logistics chain intersects with the certificate-of-destruction process in a way that creates a documentation obligation of its own.

# Registration and Reporting Obligations

The reporting obligation this instrument incorporates runs between EEA Member States and the Commission (the "questionnaire for Member States reports on the implementation of Directive 2000/53/EC"), not to private operators. *Source: Decision of the EEA Joint Committee No 15/2003, EEA Joint Committee, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:22003D0015.* *Operational implication:* no direct filing duty attaches to the workspace under this specific incorporation instrument.

# Operational System Requirements

For workspaces in the automotive vertical: track that the certificate-of-destruction regime under Directive 2000/53/EC now applies uniformly across the EU and the EEA EFTA states, since Iceland and Norway are the two EEA EFTA states this instrument specifically extends the regime to. *Operational implication:* the specific operational requirement (what the certificate of destruction must contain, who issues it) sits in the incorporated Decision itself, not in this instrument, so building a compliant process requires pulling the source document this brief has flagged rather than relying on this incorporation instrument alone.

# Confirmed Regulatory Timeline

- 31 January 2003: Decision of the EEA Joint Committee No 15/2003 adopted at Brussels. *Source: Decision of the EEA Joint Committee No 15/2003, EEA Joint Committee, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:22003D0015.*
- 1 February 2003: This Decision enters into force, provided all notifications under Article 103(1) of the EEA Agreement have been made to the EEA Joint Committee. *Source: Decision of the EEA Joint Committee No 15/2003, EEA Joint Committee, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:22003D0015.*

# Sources

- Decision of the EEA Joint Committee No 15/2003 of 31 January 2003, Official Journal L 094, 10/04/2003, EEA Joint Committee, EUR-Lex (Tier 1, primary binding text). https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:22003D0015

# Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document analyzes Council Decision 2003/278/EC of 14 April 2003 concerning the conclusion of an Agreement, in the form of an Exchange of Letters between the European Community and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, on the system of ecopoints applied to that country's transit traffic through Austria, Official Journal L 101, 23/04/2003. *Source: Council Decision 2003/278/EC, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003D0278.* This is a short approval instrument: it approves, on behalf of the Community, an Agreement that applies the Alpine transit "ecopoints" mechanism to road haulage transiting Austria under the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia's flag. The captured text does not itself set out the ecopoints calculation method or the day-to-day management rules; it references the Agreement it approves for those details.

# What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The Council approved an Agreement extending the ecopoints system, already applied within the Community's own Alpine transit framework, to transit traffic of the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia through Austria: "The Agreement between the European Community and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia in the field of transport(3), and in particular Article 12(3)(b) thereof, establishes that a system of ecopoints equivalent to that laid down by Article 11 of Protocol 9 to the Act of Accession of Austria, Finland and Sweden to the European Union shall apply." *Source: Council Decision 2003/278/EC, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003D0278.* For workspaces routing road freight through the Austrian Alpine transit corridor on vehicles registered in, or operating under transit rights tied to, the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia (now North Macedonia), this ecopoints mechanism is an environmental transit-quota system that can gate or condition passage through Austria. *Operational implication:* the specific ecopoint allocation, consumption rate per vehicle emissions class, and administrative procedure are set out in the Agreement this Decision approves, which this captured text does not reproduce; a workspace with exposure here needs that separate Agreement text, not this approval Decision alone, to plan compliant transits.

# Issues Requiring Immediate Action

**MONITORING.** Confirm whether any road-freight routing the workspace arranges through Austria involves a carrier operating under former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia transit rights, since that traffic is the specific population this ecopoints extension addresses. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a specific carrier or vehicle in the workspace's transit routing falls within the Agreement's own scope as a matter of that carrier's registration and transit-rights status.

# How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The Agreement's ecopoints mechanism runs between the Community, Austria, and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia at a state and administrative level; the carriers actually transiting Austria are the operational population the mechanism is designed to meter, while a freight forwarder arranging that carriage is not itself a party to the Agreement. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the workspace, where it selects or instructs a specific carrier for an Austria transit leg, has any obligation to confirm that carrier's ecopoints standing before booking the movement.

# Substantive Requirements

**Ecopoints extension approved.** "The Agreement in the form of an Exchange of Letters between the European Community and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia concerning the system of ecopoints to be applied to transit traffic of the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia through Austria is hereby approved on behalf of the Community." *Source: Council Decision 2003/278/EC, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003D0278.*

**Agreement signature.** "This Agreement was signed on behalf of the Community on 29 October 2002, subject to its possible conclusion at a later date in accordance with Council Decision 2003/197/EC." *Source: Council Decision 2003/278/EC, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003D0278.* *Analytical inference:* the qualification a bare "Agreement approved 2003" reading would omit is that the Agreement was already signed in October 2002 and only formally concluded, via this Decision, roughly a year and a half later.

# Registration and Reporting Obligations

This Decision itself creates no registration or reporting duty; "the method of calculation and the detailed rules and procedures for the management and control of the ecopoints" are set by the Agreement it approves, not restated here. *Source: Council Decision 2003/278/EC, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003D0278.* *Specific ecopoints administration procedure not available from primary sources as of the export date; the source document (the approved Exchange of Letters) is not in this captured pool.*

# Operational System Requirements

For workspaces routing road freight through Austria on carriage tied to the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia's transit rights: track the carrier's ecopoints standing as part of route planning for that corridor, and retrieve the underlying Agreement text (referenced but not reproduced by this Decision) before relying on this document for the mechanism's operational detail. *Operational implication:* this is a narrow, bilateral extension of an existing Alpine transit mechanism, not a general EU-wide rule; its relevance is limited to the specific transit-rights population it names.

# Confirmed Regulatory Timeline

- 29 October 2002: The Agreement in the form of an Exchange of Letters was signed on behalf of the Community, subject to its later conclusion. *Source: Council Decision 2003/278/EC, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003D0278.*
- 14 April 2003: Council Decision 2003/278/EC adopted at Luxembourg, approving the Agreement on behalf of the Community. *Source: Council Decision 2003/278/EC, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003D0278.*

# Sources

- Council Decision 2003/278/EC of 14 April 2003, Official Journal L 101, 23/04/2003, Council of the European Union, EUR-Lex (Tier 1, primary binding text). https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003D0278

# Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document analyzes the Electricity (Fuel Mix Disclosure) Regulations 2005 (S.I. 2005 No. 391), as captured in its latest available (revised) consolidated form, which modifies standard electricity supply licence conditions in Great Britain under section 33 of the Utilities Act 2000. *Source: The Electricity (Fuel Mix Disclosure) Regulations 2005, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/391.* This document is scoped to the provisions the captured text grounds: the licensee's fuel-mix and environmental-impact disclosure duty to customers, the evidence rules behind that disclosure, and the territorial extent. The Regulations implement Article 3.6 of Directive 2003/54/EC on the internal market in electricity.

# What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The Regulations insert a standard licence condition requiring every electricity supply licensee to disclose, to customers and in promotional materials, the fuel-mix and environmental-impact data behind the electricity it supplies. "These Regulations do not extend to Northern Ireland." *Source: The Electricity (Fuel Mix Disclosure) Regulations 2005, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/391.* For workspaces procuring grid electricity for warehouses, offices, or terminal facilities in Great Britain, this disclosure duty is the regulatory source of the fuel-mix percentages and the grams-of-carbon-dioxide-per-kWh figure that appear on or with an electricity bill, which the workspace can use as an input to its own Scope 2 electricity-emissions accounting. *Operational implication:* the duty runs to the licensee (the electricity supplier), not to the workspace as customer; the workspace's own use of the disclosed data for its own emissions reporting is a downstream benefit of this instrument, not an obligation it creates.

# Issues Requiring Immediate Action

**MONITORING.** Confirm that fuel-mix and carbon-dioxide-per-kWh disclosure data is being received from the workspace's electricity supplier(s) for each Great Britain site, since this is the sourced, supplier-verified figure this Regulation requires rather than a generic grid-average estimate. *Source: The Electricity (Fuel Mix Disclosure) Regulations 2005, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/391.* *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any workspace site that generates and supplies electricity of its own (for example, on-site solar sold back to the grid) is itself a licensee subject to this disclosure duty, rather than solely a disclosure recipient.

# How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The duty holder is "the licensee" under an electricity supply licence granted under section 6(1)(d) of the Electricity Act 1989; a freight-forwarding workspace purchasing electricity as a customer is not itself the licensee and carries no direct disclosure duty on the captured text. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any workspace facility with its own generation and supply arrangement could bring it within the licensee definition for that specific arrangement.

# Substantive Requirements

**Annual disclosure cycle.** A licensee that has supplied electricity for a full disclosure period discloses the required information during the following 12-month cycle: "it shall during the 12 month period commencing on 1 October immediately following the end of the disclosure period, provide the information referred to in paragraph 4: (a) at least once in the period, to each customer that receives a bill or a statement in that period, either with or on the bill or the statement; and" also in promotional materials. *Source: The Electricity (Fuel Mix Disclosure) Regulations 2005, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/391.*

**Disclosed content.** The disclosure covers each energy source's contribution to the licensee's total electricity purchased for supply, and "the environmental impact per kWh of electricity supplied resulting from the total amount of electricity purchased for supply by the licensee in terms of emissions of carbon dioxide and the production of radioactive waste." *Source: The Electricity (Fuel Mix Disclosure) Regulations 2005, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/391.*

**Rounding rule.** "The contribution referred to in sub-paragraph 4(a) must be expressed as a percentage of the total amount of electricity purchased for supply by the licensee, rounded to the nearest whole percentage point or, where the contribution is less than one percent, to one decimal place." *Source: The Electricity (Fuel Mix Disclosure) Regulations 2005, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/391.* *Operational implication:* this rounding convention is a data-quality qualification worth knowing before a workspace treats a disclosed fuel-mix percentage as precise to more than one decimal place.

**Evidence and transition rule.** The licensee generally claims a fuel-source contribution only where it holds a guarantee of origin or generator declaration; a transitional easement allowed generator declarations for renewable sources "until 1 July 2006 only," after which a guarantee of origin was required for that purpose. *Source: The Electricity (Fuel Mix Disclosure) Regulations 2005, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/391.* *Analytical inference:* the qualification a headline "generator declarations are accepted evidence" reading would omit is that this was time-limited for renewable sources, ending mid-2006; the current evidentiary standard for renewables is the guarantee of origin.

# Registration and Reporting Obligations

There is no separate registration scheme beyond the electricity supply licence itself; the reporting duty is the disclosure cycle described above, and separately the licensee provides information to the Authority (Ofgem) on request, "for the purpose of establishing whether, in the Authority's opinion, the licensee is complying or has complied with the requirements of this licence condition." *Source: The Electricity (Fuel Mix Disclosure) Regulations 2005, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/391.* *Operational implication:* this on-request power is the Authority's compliance-monitoring tool for the licensee, not a duty that reaches the workspace as a disclosure recipient.

# Operational System Requirements

For workspaces using disclosed fuel-mix and carbon-dioxide-per-kWh data in their own emissions accounting: (1) collect the disclosure data from each Great Britain electricity supplier for each disclosure period (1 April to 31 March), and (2) apply the rounding convention above when treating a fuel-mix percentage as an input figure, rather than assuming greater precision than the source data carries. *Operational implication:* this is a data-sourcing opportunity for the workspace's own Scope 2 reporting, not a compliance burden, since the workspace sits on the receiving side of the disclosure duty.

# Confirmed Regulatory Timeline

- 24th February 2005: The Electricity (Fuel Mix Disclosure) Regulations 2005 made; laid before Parliament 25th February 2005; coming into force 18th March 2005. *Source: The Electricity (Fuel Mix Disclosure) Regulations 2005, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/391.*
- 1 July 2006: End of the transitional period during which a generator declaration (rather than a guarantee of origin) was accepted evidence for a renewable-energy-source contribution. *Source: The Electricity (Fuel Mix Disclosure) Regulations 2005, UK Government (legislation.gov.uk). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/391.*

# Sources

- The Electricity (Fuel Mix Disclosure) Regulations 2005, S.I. 2005 No. 391, UK Government, legislation.gov.uk (Tier 1, primary binding text, latest available revised consolidated version). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/391
